author: Elizabeth Blessing
title: Trump and Xi only extended their trade truce to January 10, so tariffs on Chinese goods stay in place through the holidays - NewsBreak
text:
By Elizabeth Blessing ,
1 days ago
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced two months of additional breathing room in the U.S.-China trade standoff on September 24, 2026, the day President Trump hosted President Xi Jinping in Washington. The truce that had been due to expire November 10 will now run through January 10, 2027, Bessent said, meaning the tariffs already sitting on Chinese imports continue unchanged rather than escalating or coming down. That timeline covers the entire holiday shopping season.
A two-month extension, not a new deal “We will extend what we call the ‘Busan Agreement’ … that is going to be extended until Jan. 10,” Bessent said, referring to the framework the two countries first struck at an October 2025 summit in Busan, South Korea, according to a report on his remarks . The extension pushes the deadline back by two months, from November 10, 2026, to January 10, 2027, without introducing new terms beyond stretching the existing arrangement further into the new year.
An analysis from Saxo Bank of the same Washington summit described the outcome the same way: “the main result was a short extension of the existing truce,” rather than a fresh round of tariff cuts or a broader agreement. The analysis noted that on tariff relief specifically, “the detail did not arrive” at the summit, meaning the meeting produced a calendar extension without a corresponding reduction in the duties themselves.
The original Busan framework had already paired the truce on new tariff escalation with limits on China’s export controls over rare earth minerals, the materials used in electronics manufacturing, and the report on Bessent’s remarks said those limits carry forward under the extension rather than being renegotiated. Neither side described the extension as reopening any of the framework’s other terms, which according to an S&P Global Platts report on Bessent’s announcement also include a roughly 13 percent combined duty on Chinese soybean shipments, a figure separate from the broader tariff schedule covering manufactured goods.

What did not change: the tariff rates themselves An extension of the truce is not the same as a rollback of the tariffs it covers. The duties layered onto various categories of Chinese goods over 2025 and 2026, including a combined roughly 13 percent import duty on soybeans that separately applies to the agricultural side of the relationship, remain in place under the extended arrangement rather than stepping down, according to the S&P Global Platts analysis of Bessent’s announcement. Neither Bessent nor the White House described any specific tariff-rate reduction taking effect as part of the two-month extension.
The summit also left a specific technology dispute untouched. The Trump administration “announced no easing of restrictions on advanced chips or semiconductor equipment,” according to the Saxo Bank analysis, meaning export-control limits on high-end computing hardware sold to China continue alongside the tariff truce rather than being part of the trade-off.
Why the holiday shopping season is the test Retailers typically place their largest orders for the November and December selling season months in advance, which means much of the merchandise arriving on store shelves this holiday season was already priced, shipped or in transit under the tariff structure in place before the summit. Because the truce extension preserves that structure rather than lowering it, importers bringing in electronics, toys, apparel and other goods from China through the holidays will clear customs paying the same duties that applied over the summer, with no relief timed to the shopping season itself.
The new January 10, 2027 deadline sets the next point at which the arrangement could change again, whether through a further extension, a more detailed agreement, or a lapse back into higher tariffs if the two sides do not act. Bessent’s announcement did not address what happens if no further agreement is reached before that date, and neither the Treasury Department nor the White House laid out a specific negotiating timeline for the two and a half months between the summit and the new deadline.
For a household budget, the practical effect is that nothing changes on the price side of the ledger because of Wednesday’s news. Whatever a retailer’s landed cost looked like on a shipment of Chinese-made goods in August looks the same in December, since the extension neither adds a new duty nor removes an existing one. Any price movement a shopper notices this holiday season on electronics, toys or apparel sourced from China is more likely to trace back to the tariff schedule that was already in force before the summit than to anything decided at it.
A summit framed as stability, not a breakthrough Saxo Bank’s read of the Washington meeting was blunt about its scope: the visit delivered “stability, not a breakthrough,” in the analysis’s own framing, with the extension functioning as a way to keep talks going rather than resolve the underlying tariff and export-control disputes. The report on Bessent’s remarks characterized the extended framework as preserving tariff levels that remain lower than they would otherwise be without any truce in place at all, even though the extension itself did not lower the tariffs further from where they already stood going into the summit.
